The instructor was consistently respectful, polite, and considerate toward students. Their demeanor in the classroom was notably gentle and professional, which contributed to a comfortable and non-intimidating learning environment.

However, the instructional method relied almost entirely on reading from prepared notes and transcribing the same content onto the board. The lectures lacked originality, interpretation, or additional explanation beyond what was already provided in the written materials. There was little attempt to expand on the content, offer alternative perspectives, or engage students through discussion or examples.

As a result, the lectures added limited value beyond the course notes. In fact, a recorded lecture or a structured online video could have been more effective, as it would allow students to pause, revisit unclear sections, and learn at their own pace. The absence of interactive or creative teaching elements significantly reduced the overall effectiveness of the class, despite the instructor’s respectful and kind attitude.

In a course conducted in this manner, I find it difficult to justify the use of mandatory attendance, especially when attendance directly affects grading. Penalizing students for not attending—or not being able to attend—is fundamentally unfair. Academic evaluation should be based on learning outcomes, effort, and demonstrated understanding, not on physical presence in a classroom that offers little added value beyond written notes.
Students who wish to attend and benefit from the lectures should of course be free to do so, while those who prefer to study independently should not be disadvantaged for making that choice. Converting attendance into a graded component only adds unnecessary pressure and fatigue, without contributing meaningfully to the quality of learning.
Moreover, the attendance-taking process itself negatively impacts the classroom environment. Students who attend solely to sign the attendance sheet often arrive late, interrupt the lecture, and engage in activities unrelated to the course. This disrupts the flow of the class and distracts students who are genuinely trying to follow the lecture. Being interrupted by calls for signatures or movement during the session significantly reduces concentration and undermines the learning atmosphere.
Removing mandatory attendance from such courses would not lower academic standards; on the contrary, it would improve the overall quality and seriousness of the class by allowing genuinely motivated students to engage without constant disruption. Eliminating attendance-based grading would make the course fairer, more respectful of students’ circumstances, and more aligned with the principles of effective higher education.
